title: Police detain protester highlighting Hillary Clinton's racist remarks at African-American museum opening

The protester's sign refers to a video in which Hillary Clinton describes young black men as super predators and suggests that they need to be brought to heel. Trump supporter Jack Posobiec went to the Mall dressed in an orange prison outfit, a blond wig and a Hillary Clinton mask, holding a sign that read "Blacks are super predators H". The sign referred to a controversial remark Clinton made while First Lady in the 1990s. Clinton did not attend the museum opening, which was attended by President Barack Obama and former President George W. Bush. The reasons given for detaining and searching Posobiec included holding a sign, an unfounded claim that he was threatening the president by being present, holding a can of Monster, and an implied statement that he was annoying Black people with his demonstration. A separate video shows Posobiec protesting. The only people offended by his protest appear to have been the US Park Police under Obama.

title: Burning fall leaves is highly toxic for the body and the planet
text: It is autumn in the northern hemisphere, and the leaves have begun to fall and change colour. Raking leaves and burning the piles has been a common practice, but information is spreading about why the practice is very harmful to people and the planet. Burning leaves is harmful to human health. According to Wisconsin's Department of Natural Resources, burning leaves creates a large amount of dust, soot and other airborne particulates, because leaves often burn slowly. These toxic particles can reach deep into the lungs, which can cause long-term respiratory problems as well as short-term problems such as coughing, wheezing and aggravated asthma. Specifically, burning leaves produces smoke that contains carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide is deadly because it binds with hemoglobin in the bloodstream, which sharply reduces the amount of oxygen circulating through the body. Supplements that a person can take after exposure to leaf smoke are discussed later. Leaf smoke also contains benzo (a) pyrene, a known carcinogen that binds to and mutates DNA and is thought to be a major factor in cancer from cigarette smoke. In addition, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the concentrations of pollutants from leaf smoke can be higher than all other forms of air pollution combined, including factories, vehicles, and garden and lawn equipment. As an alternative to burning leaves, people can compost them or find out whether their town or city offers a leaf pick-up service.

title: Ratings be damned! 'Quantico' boss shrugs off Trump voters: it's about 'inclusion'
text: He is not backing down. Josh Safran, showrunner of ABC's Quantico, says the struggling drama will keep pushing political plots that mirror the Trump White House, even if it sends the president's supporters reaching for the remote. Safran told The Hollywood Reporter this week that in the remaining episodes of Season 2 the show becomes "a little bit of a West Wing junior," and will soon take on fake news. And there is more. THR reports: "In coming weeks, the show’s version of Trump, which Safran describes as a parallel but not a mirror image, will make his entrance, bringing with him more versions of Steve Bannon, Paul Ryan and other members of Trump’s inner circle. And Hunter Parrish (Weeds, Good Girls Revolt) has joined the series as first son Clayton Haas, a political strategist whom Safran likens to former Obama speechwriter Jon Favreau." Quantico, which already took a swipe at Trump in its first season, has seen its ratings crash by nearly 50 percent since its Season 2 opener on September 25. Moving the series from Sunday to Monday barely helped. The latest episode drew a dismal rating and just 3.31 million total viewers, trailing far behind NBC's Taken and CBS's Scorpion in the same slot. Worried? Not Safran. He insists he is not preoccupied by ratings or by whether Quantico gets a third season. Instead, he says, he is working to make the show as good as possible. Coming up, reportedly: storylines about fake news and a debate over a Muslim registry. "Regardless, the show will either come back or it won’t," he said. "I highly doubt we’re going to double in the ratings and I also highly doubt we’re going to lose half of our audience."

title: Back in the firing line! Susan Rice caught in surveillance storm
text: She has been here before. After the 2012 attack on an American diplomatic outpost in Benghazi, Libya, Susan E. Rice was at the heart of the storm, her every statement picked apart and attacked. Now she is back in the cross hairs, as questions swirl over her handling of intelligence involving President Trump's associates. A longtime Democratic foreign policy official and President Barack Obama's last national security adviser, Ms. Rice has become an inkblot test in the explosive fight over Russian meddling in last year's election. Republicans see a partisan who mined intelligence reports to spy on Mr. Trump's team. Democrats see a scapegoat, smeared for doing her job and used as a distraction from an F.B.I. investigation into Mr. Trump's associates. So what is the fuss about? Her requests for the identities of Americans swept up in electronic surveillance of foreigners, as cited in reports handed to her by intelligence agencies. Americans who were affiliated with Mr. Trump. On Tuesday, Ms. Rice came out swinging on television and Twitter. She neither confirmed nor denied making such requests, but insisted that any she might have made were proper and necessary, and no part of political espionage against the Trump campaign. "The allegation is that somehow the Obama administration officials utilized intelligence for political purposes," Ms. Rice told the journalist Andrea Mitchell on MSNBC. "That’s absolutely false." Ms. Rice said she had sometimes asked for the names of Americans whose identities were redacted in her daily intelligence briefings, so that she could understand the context of what she was being told. The purpose, she said, was "to do our jobs," but "absolutely not for any political purpose, to spy, expose, anything."

title: Irma wrecks Cuba's sugar industry: devastation across the cane fields!
text: Hurricane Irma has dealt a brutal blow to Cuba's already crumbling sugar industry, flooding and flattening a vast swath of sugar cane, state-run media reported on Monday. The scale is staggering. Some 300,000 hectares (740,000 acres) of cane were hit to different degrees, Liobel Perez, spokesman for AZCUBA, the state sugar monopoly, was quoted as stating. And the mills? He said 40 percent of the country's mills were also damaged, along with warehouses and other parts of the industry's infrastructure. This is no minor sector. Despite a steep slide in output over the last 15 years, the industry remains one of the country's most important for jobs and export earnings. The sugar harvest was due to begin in November. The monster storm spent three relentless days tearing across most of the island's northern coast, from east to west, hitting hardest in the sugar-producing provinces of central Cuba, before heading north to Florida on Sunday. Officials have only just begun to count the damage, so the report was preliminary. How much worse will it get? Cuba produced 1.8 million tonnes of sugar during the 2016-2017 season.

title: Supreme Court seats will shape the future of civil rights
text: A single Supreme Court seat can change the state of civil liberties, and the coming election could determine four seats. When 95-year-old Rosanell Eaton first registered to vote in the Jim Crow South, she was required to pass a written literacy test and recite the preamble of the Constitution from memory. Seven decades after becoming one of the first African American voters in her county, Eaton again faced obstacles to her access to the vote. Because of North Carolina's new voting restrictions, Eaton had to make 11 trips to various state agencies, traveling a total of over 200 miles, to obtain the identification she needed to vote. Eaton challenged the state's voter ID laws in a case that reached the Supreme Court. After an appeals court struck down the restrictions, the Supreme Court, in a 4–4 tie vote in August, declined for now to reinstate them, pending an eventual appeal. Eaton's case shows the role that each Supreme Court justice plays. Had one more conservative justice been sitting on the court, North Carolina voters such as Eaton would face the discriminatory barriers she challenged this November. As with many decisions in the country's history, the protection of Americans' fundamental rights depended on a single seat on the Supreme Court. The court decided the Shelby County case in 2013 by one vote. That decision gutted the Voting Rights Act, a landmark achievement of the 1960s civil rights movement, and allowed North Carolina to establish these discriminatory voting restrictions in the first place.

title: Bank run panic, then rescue: why Bulgaria still loves the E.U.!
text: Panic. In the summer of 2014, Bulgaria was gripped by a bank run, and Lyubomir Vassilev was terrified. Unemployed and living off a compensation package from a workplace accident, he was cut off from his bank account and joined others in angry street protests when a troubled lender collapsed into bankruptcy, setting off a financial — and political — crisis. Months of hardship followed. His parents had to borrow money from relatives just to help him survive. Finally, Mr. Vassilev got his $6,000 back. "After the bank went bankrupt," he said, "I lost trust in the banking system." Who did he blame? Bulgaria's leaders. And like many of his compatriots, he credited the European Union with ending the crisis. That is a striking contrast. Across much of Western Europe, critics rage against distant and unfeeling technocrats in Brussels who enforce arcane rules to the letter, with little grasp of local nuances and needs. Britain's vote in June to leave the bloc dealt a stinging blow to regional unity at a time when confidence in the European Union was already sinking. But Mr. Vassilev and his fellow citizens tell a very different story — one of regional officials who hold domestic authorities to account, set higher standards and are more trustworthy than their local counterparts. Bulgaria joined the European Union in 2007, along with Romania. Back then, polling showed only a slim majority in favor of membership, hoping it would strengthen the Balkan country's economy and political institutions. And today? Bulgaria is still the bloc's poorest member state, with a per capita gross domestic product about half the regional average.

Although the suspects' actions were horrible, people are not sentenced to death for assault or kidnapping. Had they murdered the victim, Lahren would have had a case for the death penalty. They did not. Lahren also questioned parenting in inner cities, a coded reference to black people. "Times like these, we have to wonder, where are the parents?" she said.

title: Huge win for abortion-rights side: Iowa Supreme Court freezes waiting period!
text: A dramatic legal blow for the law's backers. The Iowa Supreme Court has kept in place a block on a three-day waiting period for women seeking an abortion until a legal challenge is over, a decision cheered by abortion-rights advocates. The provision was signed into law in May by former Republican Governor Terry Branstad, part of a package of new rules that also banned most abortions after 20 weeks. The waiting period was challenged earlier this year by the American Civil Liberties Union of Iowa and Planned Parenthood. And the state? The Iowa state attorney general's office could not be reached for comment on Tuesday. The U.S. Supreme Court legalized abortion in 1973, although states can limit and regulate abortions. And limit they have. U.S. state legislatures enacted a startling 41 new abortion restrictions in the first half of 2017, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive health group that supports abortion rights. Planned Parenthood on Tuesday hailed the court's decision, issued on Monday, to keep in place an earlier stay on the requirement that women wait 72 hours before having an abortion. "This ruling ensures that women in Iowa will have continued access to the health care they need throughout the course of this lawsuit," said Susan Allen, a spokeswoman for Planned Parenthood of the Heartland. The fight has been bruising. A lower court had earlier upheld the disputed provision, noting that 27 states have imposed waiting periods for abortion, ranging from 18 to 72 hours, the Des Moines Register reported on Tuesday. And in May, Planned Parenthood said it would shut four of its 12 clinics in Iowa because of another Iowa measure that cut off public money for family planning services to abortion providers. What comes next?

title: Clooney unloads on Trump at César Awards: 'comfort to our enemies'!
text: George Clooney let rip. At the César Film Awards ceremony in Paris on Friday night, the actor launched into a blistering Trump rant, claiming that the president is alarming America's allies and giving "comfort to our enemies." While accepting his honorary award, Clooney said, "I was thinking about Edward R. Murrow," referencing his 2005 film Good Night, and Good Luck, "as we find ourselves nostalgic for when America was great and when the news wasn’t fake." "We must not confuse dissent for disloyalty," Clooney continued, quoting Murrow. "We must not walk in fear of one another. We must not be driven by fear into an age of unreason." Then came the political punch. "The actions of this president have caused alarm and dismay amongst our allies abroad and given considerable comfort to our enemies." "And whose fault is that?" the Money Monster star asked, never once naming Trump. "Not really his. He didn’t create this situation of fear, he merely exploited it, and rather successfully." Brutal! The actor's charged speech came just days after he branded Trump and White House chief strategist Steve Bannon the real "Hollywood elitists." Pointing to actress Meryl Streep's infamous speech at the Golden Globes last month, Clooney insisted Hollywood celebrities have a right to preach politics. "When Meryl [Streep] spoke, everyone on that one side said, ‘Well, that’s elitist Hollywood speaking,’" Clooney said in an interview with French news outlet Canal Plus. Trump, the actor added, "collects $120,000 a year from his Screen Actors Guild pension fund. He is a Hollywood elitist." And Bannon? Clooney said Bannon, who has produced 16 films, is a "failed film writer and director." Ouch!

title: Giuliani defends Trump's remarks on tape; Tapper rejects his explanation
text: A tape in which Donald Trump boasts about sexually assaulting women has caused turmoil in the Republican Party this weekend. Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani has sought to minimize the tape, arguing that men talk that way. CNN's Jake Tapper did not accept this explanation. Appearing on State of the Union on Sunday morning, the former New York City mayor tried unsuccessfully to persuade viewers that the remarks were locker talk and that voters should still support Trump, even though he brags about grabbing women by the p*ssy. "This is talk, and gosh almighty, he who hasn't sinned, throw the first stone," Giuliani said of Trump's remarks on the leaked tape from 2005. Tapper interrupted him and rejected Giuliani's argument. "Mr. Mayor, I have never said that. I have never done that," Tapper said. "I am happy to throw a stone. I have been in locker rooms, I have been a member of a fraternity. I have never heard any man, ever, brag about being able to maul women because they get away with it." Giuliani continued to maintain that this is how men are. "The fact is men, at times, talk like that. Not all men." Tapper asked the former mayor whether he had ever said such things, but Giuliani continued speaking and did not acknowledge the question. Giuliani then said: "I'm not justifying it." He did not deny having made similar comments himself. Earlier in the interview, Giuliani said that Trump had apologized for his behavior and was likely to do so again during the upcoming debate on Sunday night.
